events.text: Dark, and warm, and red. Not the red of anything you have seen, because you have seen nothing: the red of sand that holds the heat of the mountain long after the sun has gone. You are inside a shell, inside the sand, at the back of a cave. Far below, through the rock, something runs and runs and never stops talking. Nobody is sitting on you. Nobody needs to.

choices.text: Listen to the river

effects.log: It goes south. You can hear that it goes south, the way you will one day hear that a king is lying. You listen until you know its every stone.

choices.text: Listen to the mountain

effects.log: Under the sand the mountain is full of slow things: gold sleeping in its veins, jade thinking green thoughts. It hums. You hum back, inside the shell, without a beak to hum with.

choices.text: Listen for anyone at all

effects.log: Nobody. And then, so far off it might be inside you, something else listening back. Another shell. Another sand. You do not know yet that you will spend a long time finding out what it was.

events.text: The shell is too small. It was the whole world in the spring, and now it presses on your back like a lid. You are folded up in it with your knees round your ears and something on your face, hard and new, that wants very much to hit something.

choices.text: Hit the shell. Hard

effects.log: Tap. Tap. TAP. A crack like a hair, and through it, red light. You hit it until your new beak aches and the light is the size of a grain of rice. Then you rest, and hit it again.

choices.text: Push with your back, slowly

effects.log: You push and breathe and push. The shell gives along a seam you did not know was there, as if it had always meant to open there and was only waiting to be asked properly.

choices.text: Sing at it

effects.log: You do not know what singing is. You do it anyway, a thin wet peep inside the egg, and the shell, which has heard nothing in a year but the river, cracks from end to end in surprise.

events.text: You stand on red sand on two legs that have not agreed yet which of them is in charge. You are damp, drab, the colour of a farmyard hen that has been rained on, and very loud. The cave goes back into the mountain in veins of gold and green. It goes forward to a mouth full of light. Nobody comes. Nobody is anywhere. You look round twice, to be sure.

choices.text: Shout, to see who answers

effects.log: You shout. The cave shouts back, three times, smaller each time. That is the cave, not anyone. You shout again anyway. It is good to know that you can.

choices.text: Peck the gold in the wall

effects.log: It is hard and cold and tastes of nothing. Humans will kill one another for it for a thousand years. You lose interest in it before noon.

choices.text: Go to the mouth of the cave and look out

effects.log: Mountains below mountains, in layers of blue, and the red river winding south between them like a thread somebody dropped. All of it is quiet. You decide, at once and for no reason, that you like it.

events.text: Nobody comes. A whole season, and nobody: no parent with a worm, no flock, no other chick. A hen in a farmyard would have died of it. You find, turning it over in the evening at the cave mouth, that you do not mind. You are not lonely. You are only alone, which is a different shape, and you fit it.

choices.text: Decide that this is how it is meant to be

effects.log: It is. The old book that humans will one day write about you says only that you eat and drink as you please and sing and dance by yourself. Nobody in the book ever comes to the cave either.

choices.text: Decide that somebody is coming, one day

effects.log: Somebody is. Not for a long time, and not to this cave. But you sing a little louder at dawn from then on, in case it carries.

choices.text: Stop thinking about it and eat sand

effects.log: Sand is not food. You find this out thoroughly. (-2 health)

events.text: The morning you leave the Cinnabar Cave for good you do not plan it. You are at the mouth, beating your new wings at the wind for practice, and the wind takes you at your word. The red sand drops away. The gold and the jade go small. The red river turns under you like a ribbon, and beyond the last mountain there is a country: paddies, smoke, roofs, and trees, and every tree in it a question.

choices.text: Follow the river south

effects.log: You follow it the way you listened to it inside the egg, every bend of it, until it meets the sea. Then you turn north and begin, very slowly, to learn the land.

choices.text: Fly as high as you can, to see it all

effects.log: Up until the cold hurts your new feathers. The whole peninsula lies under you like a hand, the mountains its knuckles. A farmer below sees a dot of five colours and tells nobody, because who would believe it.

choices.text: Look back at the cave once

effects.log: A dark mouth on a red mountain. You will come back to it once, at the very end, if heaven wishes it. You do not know that. You only know you wanted to look.

events.text: Something is wrong with your feet. They will not stay still. The sand is warm, and the light from the cave mouth falls in one bright square, and your feet keep stepping into it and out of it, in and out, and your wings, which are not wings yet, keep lifting.

choices.text: Let your feet do it

effects.log: In, out, turn, wings up. In, out, turn. You dance in the square of light until it moves off the sand and up the wall. Nobody sees. It was not for anyone.

choices.text: Make them stop, and think about it first

effects.log: You hold your feet still with great effort. They want to dance. You ask yourself why. You get no answer, and the light moves on, and you are a little sorry.

choices.text: Sing to keep time

effects.log: Peep, and step. Peep, peep, and turn. It is not a song yet. It is the bones of one, and the cave keeps the time for you by echoing.

events.text: You have the steps now. Five of them, in an order that is right for reasons you cannot say, and a sixth at the end that is a kind of bow. You dance them every morning at the cave mouth, for nobody, and every morning you find you have done them a little better for nobody than the day before.

choices.text: Add a step

effects.log: You try seven, and it is wrong. You try a different seventh, and it is wrong. You go back to six and find that the sixth was always the bow. Some things are finished when they are small.

choices.text: Dance in the rain on the ledge

effects.log: The rain flattens your down to your skin and you dance anyway, slipping, until a rock-dove on the cliff opposite stops preening to watch. You stop. It looks away. You both pretend. (-3 health)

choices.text: Dance with your eyes shut

effects.log: With your eyes shut there is no cave and no light, only the steps and the river under the mountain. You do not fall once. You did not need to see. That is worth knowing.

events.text: One evening, halfway through the steps, you notice that you have learned to dance before you have learned to fly. Your wings can lift and turn and bow. They cannot yet take you anywhere. Every other bird in the world, you suspect, did this the other way round.

choices.text: Decide the dance was the right thing to learn first

effects.log: It was. A bird that can fly can go anywhere. A bird that can dance knows when it has arrived. You will need the second far more than the first.

choices.text: Practise flying, ashamed

effects.log: You fling yourself off the ledge and come down on the sand like a dropped mitten. Again. Again. By dark you can glide the length of the cave, and you dance the six steps anyway before you sleep. (-4 health)

choices.text: Do both: dance on the wind at the cave mouth

ok.log: For three heartbeats the wind holds you up off the ledge and you dance on nothing. Then it lets you down, gently, as if it had enjoyed it too.

fail.log: The wind takes the dance and keeps it and drops you in a thorn bush below the cave. You climb back up in the dark, much wiser, short a few downy feathers. (-5 health)

events.text: You have looked at your own reflection in the pool at the foot of the cliff and come to a conclusion: you are brown. Not even a good brown. The brown of the dust under a granary. And yet this morning, under your left wing, where nobody can see it but you, there is one feather the colour of the sky an hour after dawn.

choices.text: Show it to the whole valley

effects.log: You stand on a rock with your wing held out at an angle that is not comfortable. Nothing in the valley notices. A beetle walks past. You fold the wing, quite pleased anyway.

choices.text: Hide it until there are more

effects.log: One blue feather is an accident. Two is a pattern. You keep your wing folded and wait, and every evening you lift it a little to check.

choices.text: Pull it out to look at it properly

effects.log: It hurts more than you expected. It is bluer than you expected. You lay it on the rock and it lies there like a piece of sky that fell. By the next new moon, three more have come in where it was. (-2 health)

events.text: A grey heron stands in the paddy at the foot of the hills, on one leg, as if it were waiting for the rice to apologise. It looks down at you, brown and fluffy with three blue feathers coming in crooked, and opens its long beak and laughs: a harsh sound, like a cart wheel that needs grease.

choices.text: Laugh back

effects.log: You laugh at it, a chick's laugh, a squeak with ideas. The heron stops, surprised. Nobody has ever laughed at the heron. It goes back to waiting for the rice, a little less sure of itself.

choices.text: Ignore it and keep walking

effects.log: You walk past the whole length of the paddy without looking. The heron laughs louder, for longer, and then stops, because there is nobody to laugh at. That is what laughter needs: somebody to land on.

choices.text: Stand on one leg beside it, exactly the same

effects.log: You fall over twice. The third time you stay up. You and the heron stand side by side in the paddy on one leg each, saying nothing, all afternoon. It is the most companionable thing that has happened to you.

events.text: It happens in one moult, the summer you are nearly grown. The brown comes out of you in handfuls and drifts down the cliff. Under it there is blue, and white, and red, and black, and a yellow like the middle of a chrysanthemum, and a tail that keeps on growing after everything else has stopped. The heron is in the paddy when you fly over. It does not laugh. It looks up for a long time with its beak a little open.

choices.text: Land beside the heron, on one leg

effects.log: You come down in the paddy beside it and stand on one leg. The heron, after a long time, bows its long neck, very slightly. Then it goes back to waiting for the rice. Some things are said once.

choices.text: Fly on without looking down

effects.log: You do not need the heron to stop laughing. You find that out as you fly over it: that you do not need anything from it at all. It is a lighter feeling than the feathers.

choices.text: Look at yourself in the paddy water instead

effects.log: Five colours. Blue at the wings, red at the breast, yellow at the belly, black and white where they cross. The water shows you, then a frog jumps and breaks it. You will not see yourself that clearly again for years.

events.text: The first real hunger. The seed that was in the sand round your egg is long gone, and the cold has got into your hollow bones, and the farmyards below the hill smell of warm straw and grain. A sparrow lands on your branch. It has brought you something in its beak, the way sparrows bring things to sparrows: a beakful of yellow millet. It puts it down in front of you and looks proud.

choices.text: Refuse it

effects.log: You look at the millet. You do not know why, but you know you do not eat it. You push it back with your beak. The sparrow looks at you as if you had spat on its doorstep, and flies off without its millet. (-6 health)

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: It is warm in your crop and it is wrong, both at once, and the wrongness lasts longer than the warmth. The sparrow watches you eat with great satisfaction. Something in your feathers goes a little dull. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Refuse it, and thank the sparrow

effects.log: You push the millet back, and then you bow to the sparrow, low, the way the sixth step of the dance bows. The sparrow does not understand at all. But it understands the bow. It takes its millet and goes, puzzled, not offended. (-6 health)

events.text: The sparrow comes back the next morning with its whole family. Seven of them, in a row on your branch, and seven beakfuls of millet laid in a row in front of you like a bride's gifts. They have decided you are ill. Sparrows believe that nothing is wrong with anybody that millet will not mend.

choices.text: Refuse all seven, kindly

effects.log: One at a time, with a bow for each. By the seventh the sparrows are bowing back. They take their millet and go away discussing you in low chirps. You are hungrier, and you have seven acquaintances. (-4 health)

choices.text: Take one beakful, to be polite

effects.log: One. Just to be polite. The sparrows cheer in their way and leave you the rest, and you sit with six beakfuls of millet in front of you all day and do not touch them, which is somehow worse. (-4 purity)

choices.text: Explain, as well as a chick can

ok.log: You peep and point your beak at the bamboo on the far hill, over and over. The oldest sparrow cocks its head. "Bamboo," it says at last, to the others, in sparrow. "It wants bamboo. It is mad." They forgive you for being mad. Sparrows are very forgiving of the mad.

fail.log: You peep and point and they nod and push the millet closer. You give up. They leave, satisfied that they have done their best for a poor sick thing. (-3 health)

events.text: Snow on the branch, snow on the hill, and nothing in your crop for three days. The sparrows have stopped bringing millet. The farmyard below has a heap of it under the eaves of the mill, gold in the grey, and the whole sparrow nation goes in and out of the mill door all day. A sparrow, the old saying will go, never passes a mill. You are not a sparrow. You are, today, very nearly one.

choices.text: Fly a thousand li hungry instead

effects.log: You fly south over three ranges of hills on an empty crop until you find a single old bamboo clump with a little seed still in the husks. It is not enough. It is the right thing. You will remember the taste of that seed with the hunger in it all your life. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go into the mill

effects.log: Warm, gold, dusty, and full of sparrows, who make room for you with great delight. You eat. Nobody in the mill thinks anything is wrong. That is what is wrong. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Sit on the branch and sing instead of eating

ok.log: You sing until the hunger is a long way off, like a village seen from a ridge. The miller below comes out to listen, holding a sieve, and forgets what the sieve was for. (-5 health)

fail.log: The song comes out thin and the hunger does not go anywhere. You sit it out, shaking, until the snow stops. (-10 health)

events.text: The sparrow who first brought you millet is old now, for a sparrow, which is four winters. It sits on your branch more often, and talks less. Today it has brought nothing. It only sits close, feathers puffed, and looks at the farmyard where it was hatched.

choices.text: Sit close to it until evening

effects.log: You sit wing to wing till dark. It says, in sparrow, that you were the strangest thing it ever fed. You say, as well as you can, that it was the kindest thing anyone ever did for you, and that you are sorry you could not eat it. It understands the second part.

choices.text: Bring it a bamboo seed

effects.log: One seed out of your store, carried all the way in your beak. The sparrow looks at it, then at you, and eats it with enormous ceremony. "Hard," it says. "Hard and dry. You are mad." It is the last thing it says to you.

choices.text: Sing it the six steps of your song

effects.log: You sing and the old sparrow listens with its eyes half shut. In spring there is a nest of young sparrows under the mill eaves, and one of them, when it is grown, sings a phrase that no sparrow has ever sung before.

events.text: A lean spring. A girl in the farmyard below scatters millet for the hens, and a handful, by accident or not, goes up onto the low branch where you sit. It lies there in a little golden heap. The girl looks up at you, shading her eyes, and smiles, and goes back in. It was a kindness. It is also millet.

choices.text: Leave it for the sparrows

effects.log: You hop one branch higher. The sparrows come within the minute and the millet is gone. The girl, when she looks out again, thinks you ate it, and is happy. That is as close to eating it as you will go.

choices.text: Eat it. The girl meant it

effects.log: You eat it because she meant it. It is not a good reason. It is not a bad one either. Your breast feathers know the difference, and say so, quietly, for a long time. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Push it off the branch, back into the yard

effects.log: It falls back among the hens like a small gold rain. The hens are delighted. The girl is puzzled. You are hungry, and sure.

events.text: A dead pine on the shoulder of the hill, white as a bone, and on its lowest branch an owl the colour of bark. It has a rat. The rat has been dead for some time. The owl holds it under one foot as if it were a seal of office. You are only flying past, low, on your way to the bamboo. The owl looks up, sees you, and its feathers go out round it like a cloak.
events.arc: The Owl and the Rotten Rat

choices.text: Fly on. You were going to the bamboo

effects.log: "HSSS!" says the owl behind you, very loud, to the whole hill. "HSSS! Not my rat! You shall not have my rat!" You did not want its rat. You fly on, puzzled, to the bamboo.

choices.text: Stop on the next branch and look at the rat

effects.log: "HSSS!" The owl hunches over the rat until it is nearly sitting on it. You look at the rat. It is green in places. You look at the owl. You do not understand what it thinks you are, but you are fairly sure you are not that.

choices.text: Bow to the owl and its rat

effects.log: You bow politely. The owl takes this as a trick, and says "Hsss!" all the more. A bow is a strange thing to give a creature that guards a rotten rat. It cannot take it. It has no free foot.

events.text: The owl follows you. Not close: a tree behind, a ridge behind, always at dusk. When you land in a bamboo grove, it lands in the nearest dead tree and watches. It has a new rat now, or the old one is wearing well. Every time you turn your head, it hisses.
events.arc: The Owl and the Rotten Rat

choices.text: Lead it on a long flight, for the fun of it

effects.log: Over three valleys and back, at dusk, with the owl labouring behind with its rat. It arrives at the dead pine an hour after you, too out of breath to hiss. You sit and wait for it, politely. It hisses, eventually.

choices.text: Ignore it entirely

effects.log: A whole season of being followed, and you do not look round once. The owl finds this unbearable. It hisses louder, at nothing, until the crows of the hill complain.

choices.text: Land beside it and say, as clearly as you can: no rat

ok.log: You say it in bird, and the owl, after a very long stare, says in bird: "Everyone wants the rat." "Not everyone," you say. It does not believe you. But it has spoken to you now, and it cannot unspeak it.

fail.log: It hisses so hard it nearly falls off the branch, and then strikes at you with its free foot. You leave with a scratch on your cheek and no conversation. (-3 health)

events.text: You find the owl in a bad way: caught by one wing in a farmer's hemp net, hanging upside down from a pear tree with its rat still clutched in one foot. It sees you and does not hiss. It is too tired to hiss. The farmer's lamp is coming up the path.
events.arc: The Owl and the Rotten Rat

choices.text: Pick the net open with your beak

ok.log: Three knots, a fourth, and the owl drops onto the grass and lies there with its rat, looking at you upside down. "Why?" it says. "You could have had the rat." You leave before the lamp arrives. It will never understand it, and it will never forget it.

fail.log: The knots will not give, and then the farmer is there with his lamp and you have to fly. He takes one look at the owl, says a rude word about owls, and cuts it loose and throws it into the dark. It lands hard. It lives. (-5 health)

choices.text: Tell it to drop the rat and pull

effects.log: "Drop the rat," you say, "and use both feet." The owl stares at you with horror. It would sooner hang. It does hang, until the farmer comes and cuts the net and keeps it, and the owl goes off into the night still holding its rat, one wing trailing.

choices.text: Leave it. It would not thank you

effects.log: You fly on. Later you hear the farmer shout, and a scuffle, and later still, a long way off in the dark, a very small, very offended "hsss." It got away. It always will. Things like that do.

events.text: The owl has learned to speak. Not bird: human. It sits in the eaves of the county office in the town below the hill, night after night, listening to the clerks, and it practises on you when you pass. "Taxes," it says. "Rank. Post. Salary." It says them the way it holds the rat.
events.arc: The Owl and the Rotten Rat

choices.text: Ask it what a post is

effects.log: "A post," says the owl, "is a rat that sits in a chair." It is very pleased with this. You think about it for a long time on the way to the bamboo, and decide that the owl is wiser than it knows, and less wise than it thinks.

choices.text: Tell it you will never want any of those

effects.log: "Everyone says that," says the owl, "before they are hungry." You have been hungry. You still do not want any of them. The owl writes you down, somewhere behind its eyes, as a liar.

choices.text: Teach it a better word

effects.log: "Enough," you say. It cannot say it. It tries, for a whole night, and every time the word comes out as "more". Some birds are built that way.

events.text: The owl has found a minister. A thin, careful man from the capital, sent down to count the county's granaries, who keeps late hours and likes the owl on his window frame, because it agrees with everything he fears. The owl comes to the dead pine once more, to tell you, with its rat. "I have a master now," it says. "Do not come to his roof. I will know."
events.arc: The Owl and the Rotten Rat

choices.text: Wish it well, honestly

effects.log: "I hope the rat is a good one," you say. It looks at you a long time, trying to find the trick in it. It cannot find one. That frightens it more than a trick would have. It flies to the capital with its minister, and you will see it again.

choices.text: Say, quietly: Hsss

effects.log: You say it as softly as you can, the way it said it to you the first time. The owl starts so hard it drops the rat. It picks it up again at once. You have said its only word back to it. It will remember that. One day, so will you.

choices.text: Say nothing, and fly

effects.log: You leave it on the dead pine with its rat and its master. Behind you it hisses, once, out of habit. It will go to the capital. Owls that find ministers always do.

events.text: The dead pine on the hill is empty now. The owl has gone to the capital with its minister. In the hollow where it slept you find a heap of small grey bones, years of rats, very neatly kept, and on top of them, as if left for you, one ordinary bamboo seed.
events.arc: The Owl and the Rotten Rat

choices.text: Eat the seed

effects.log: It is a good seed. You do not know how the owl got it, or why. Perhaps it was trying, in the only language it has, to say: I know what you eat. Perhaps it was a trap. It was only a seed.

choices.text: Leave the seed on the bones

effects.log: You leave it where it lies. Some gifts are better left as gifts, unopened. When you come back years later the seed has sprouted in the hollow of the dead pine, a thin green blade among the bones.

events.text: Downriver, on the slope above a village, there is one old clump of bamboo that has done something bamboo almost never does. It has flowered. Pale, ragged, drooping things like the tassels of a mourning hat hang all along its stems, and under them, in the dust, lie seeds like small hard grains of rice. You know them from the sand round your egg, the last of which you ate long ago. You have never seen where they come from.

choices.text: Eat. Now

effects.log: It is hard, and dry, and tastes of nothing you have words for. It tastes like the morning. For the first time since the egg, your crop is full of the right thing, and every feather on you settles as if it had been waiting.

choices.text: Gather first, eat after

effects.log: You carry seed up to a crack in the rocks, beakful after beakful, all day, and only at dusk eat one. One is enough to know. You will gather like this all your life, and the store will be your life.

choices.text: Sing to the bamboo first

effects.log: It seems rude to eat without thanking it. You sing the six steps' song to the old clump, and then you eat, slowly. The bamboo, which flowers once in a few years and then dies, has been thanked, at least once.

events.text: The old clump is dying. It happens fast, the way the bamboo-cutters say it does: after the flower, the stems go yellow, then the colour of old straw, and the leaves rattle like paper. Two cutters from the village stand under it with their sickles hanging and look at it the way you look at someone who has stopped breathing.

choices.text: Stay and listen to them

effects.log: "Sixty years my father cut this clump," says the older one. "Never saw it flower. Now it flowers and dies the same year." "Bad luck," says the younger. "Or good," says the older, looking up at you, "for somebody."

choices.text: Take the last of the seed before the rats do

effects.log: You clear the dust under the dying stems seed by seed. The rats are already coming, you can smell them in the stones. You leave them nothing. It is the first time you understand that your food is someone else's funeral.

choices.text: Sit in the dying clump all day

effects.log: You sit among the yellow stems while they rattle. Nobody should die with nobody there. The cutters, seeing a bird sit there all day, decide it is mourning, and they are right, and they tell the village, and nobody believes them.

events.text: A year later, the rats. They came for the seed you left, and there was not enough, and so they have gone down into the village and into the granary and into the rice in the fields. The cutters' families eat thin gruel this winter. You learned it this year: a flowering is a feast for you and a famine for someone else, and the rats carry the bill from one to the other.

choices.text: Watch the village, and remember it

effects.log: You sit on the hill and watch thin smoke from every chimney. You will see this again, larger, all over the peninsula. Next time you will at least know what is coming.

choices.text: Give the village back some of your seed

effects.log: You drop seed in the yard of the poorest house, beakful by beakful, at night. The family finds it and cannot think what it is. The grandmother boils it with a little barley. It is not much. It is something.

choices.text: Hunt the rats off the granary

ok.log: You come down on the granary roof at dusk, all five colours spread, shrieking. The rats have never seen anything like it. Neither has the village. It is the first story anyone tells about you.

fail.log: There are hundreds of them and one of you. You come away with a bitten foot and a new respect for rats. (-6 health)

events.text: Ten years on, you fly over the slope where the old clump died. The cutters' children are cutters now. And where the dead stems stood there are new green shoots, thin as chopsticks, coming up out of the rotten old ones, not a single flower among them. It will be another sixty years.

choices.text: Mark the place for later

effects.log: You fix it in your memory: the slope, the village, the shape of the hill. In a few years you will come back and be here first. A phoenix has a long time to keep appointments.

choices.text: Land and greet the young cutters

effects.log: One of them looks up and drops his sickle. "It is the mourning bird," he says, "from my father's story." The other one says there is no such bird. You stay just long enough to make them argue for the rest of their lives.

events.text: You have eaten bamboo seed and nothing else for years now. One morning you find you can tell, from the air, which groves are thinking about flowering: a smell like dry rice straw, a little yellow at the tips, a stillness in the stems. Nobody taught you. It came with the seed.

choices.text: Fly the country and count the groves

effects.log: Three groves in the south, thinking. One in the west, nearly decided. None will flower this year. You collect what the stray clumps give and fly home with your list in your head, like a granary-keeper.

choices.text: Keep the knowledge to yourself

effects.log: It is your secret and the bamboo's. Humans read flowering bamboo as an omen. They do not know it is only bamboo being bamboo, once in a lifetime. Neither, sometimes, do you.

events.text: A spring in the rocks above a village, under a pine bent like an old back. You land to drink only because you are thirsty, and the water stops you with your beak still in it. It is sweet. Not with honey: sweet like cooked rice when you chew it a long time, sweet like the milk you never had. Every other water you have tasted was only wet.

choices.text: Drink until you are full

effects.log: You drink, and something in you that you did not know was dusty comes clean. You understand now why the thing in you refused the millet. It was waiting for this. (+2 purity)

choices.text: Drink a little and taste it slowly

effects.log: One sip, held. Pine, stone, cold, and under it that sweetness, like a word in a language you were born knowing. You will go looking for that taste for a thousand years. (+2 purity)

choices.text: Look at who else drinks here

effects.log: A small stone by the spring with a bowl on it, and the bowl full. The village draws the first water of every morning here, before anyone else has touched it, and sets it out for the sky. You are drinking from their prayer. You drink less. (+1 purity)

events.text: The village under the spring calls it the milk spring. Women with water jars come up the path at dawn, and an old woman rinses her bowl first and sets it on the stone for the sky. Children are told that a sweet spring rises only where the land is ruled well, and that if the magistrate ever turns cruel, it will dry up. They say it the way children say things: half joke, half oath.

choices.text: Drink only after they have gone

effects.log: You wait in the pine every morning until the last jar has gone down the path. The spring is theirs first. You are a guest in it. The old woman leaves her bowl a little fuller every day, and does not know why she does.

choices.text: Let them see you drink, once

effects.log: A child with a jar stops dead on the path. You lift your head from the spring, five colours, and look at her. She does not shout. She goes home and tells her grandmother, who tells her that is what the spring is for.

choices.text: Sit in the pine and listen to the women talk

effects.log: The price of salt. A wedding in the next valley. A son gone for a soldier. The new magistrate, who is said to be honest, and very thin, and to like his tea weak. You learn more about the land in a season of listening than in a year of flying.

events.text: Some years later a new magistrate comes to the county, a heavy man with a heavy seal, and the first thing he does is double the grain tax and the second is have a man beaten in the yard for being slow to bow. That spring, the milk spring runs thin. By midsummer it is a damp stain on the rock. The old woman's bowl stands on the stone, dry.

choices.text: Leave, as the children said the spring would

effects.log: You fly from the pine in full sight of the path, and stay away while it is dry. The village notices both things, the dry spring and the bird gone, and puts them together, and says so, quietly, in the fields where the magistrate cannot hear.

choices.text: Stay and drink from the last of it

effects.log: You drink the last sweet mouthfuls from a crack in the rock, and then there are none. You are not the cause, and you could not stop it. You only understand now that the children were right. (-4 health)

choices.text: Drink from the magistrate's new well instead

effects.log: His well is deep, and the water is clean enough, and it tastes of iron and the rope. You drink anyway. Something under your breast feathers turns its face away. (-5 purity)

events.text: The heavy magistrate has been called away, in disgrace, they say, over a granary that was full on paper and empty in fact. And that same spring, on a morning of mist, the stone under the old pine is wet again, and then dripping, and then there is a thread of water running down to the path. The old woman's granddaughter sets out the bowl.

choices.text: Come back, and drink at dawn

effects.log: The first sweet water in years. The granddaughter sees you from the path and does not run home this time. She sits on the stone and watches you drink, and you let her. (+2 purity)

choices.text: Watch from the ridge, and let them have it first

effects.log: The whole village comes up the path that morning, every jar it owns. You watch from the ridge. It is their spring. It came back for them. You were only one of the ones it came back for.

events.text: A farmyard on a morning-sun slope, and in the corner of it, by the well, a young paulownia: five years old, they will tell you, because it was planted the spring the daughter of the house was born, and it is already taller than the roof. Leaves as wide as fans. Purple flowers like little bells. It is the first tree you have ever wanted to sit in. You land. Below, a small child with a gourd dipper looks up at you, and does not shout.

choices.text: Stay. This tree is yours

effects.log: It holds you as if it was planted for you. Perhaps it was. {npc} watches you all morning and tells the tree, quite seriously, that you are welcome.

choices.text: Stay, and look the child in the eye

mem.note: came to my tree

effects.log: You look down. {npc} looks up. Neither of you is in a hurry. Then {he} goes indoors and comes out with {his} grandmother, and by then you are only a tail among the leaves.

choices.text: Stay, but keep to the high branches

effects.log: Up where the leaves are widest, out of sight of the house. Only {npc} knows you are there, and {he} tells nobody, because nobody would believe {him}, and because a secret is a thing of {his} own.

events.text: {npc} talks to you every morning. {He} stands under the paulownia with the gourd dipper and tells you everything: the hen that laid two eggs, the brother who pulled {his} hair, the moon, which {he} thinks is following {him} home. {He} does not wait for answers. {He} only wants the tree to know.

choices.text: Listen, every morning

mem.note: listened every morning

effects.log: You learn the names of every hen. You learn that a brother is a kind of weather. You learn that a child alone in a yard is very rarely alone in {his} own head. {npc} grows taller, and the tree grows taller faster.

choices.text: Drop a leaf at {his} feet, as an answer

mem.note: answered me

effects.log: One wide leaf, spinning down. {npc} picks it up and holds it like a letter. From then on, if {he} asks a question and a leaf falls, it means yes. You are careful which questions you let a leaf fall on.

choices.text: Sing back, once, softly

mem.note: sang to me from the tree

ok.log: Three notes, only for the yard. {npc} stands absolutely still, the dipper dripping, and then sings them back, wrong, and laughs. That evening {he} sings them to the hens. The hens are not impressed.

fail.log: You sing just as the grandmother comes out with the washing, looks up into the tree, sees nothing but leaves, and says the wind has got into the paulownia. {npc} says nothing, and grins at the leaves.

events.text: A summer storm comes up the valley at night and takes the roof off the barn. In the morning {npc}, taller now, is in the yard in the rain with {his} arms round the paulownia's trunk, as if {he} could hold it up. One great branch is cracked. Through the rain {he} is looking up for you.

choices.text: Come down to the cracked branch, where {he} can see

mem.note: stayed in my tree through the storm

effects.log: You come down out of the high leaves to the broken limb, wet through, and sit on it. {npc} sees you, lets go of the trunk, and stands there crying with relief in the rain. You were never in danger. {He} did not know that.

choices.text: Hold the cracked branch with your whole weight against the wind

ok.log: You brace on it all morning with your wings half open, and the crack does not spread. The grandfather binds it with straw rope at noon. It heals crooked, the strongest branch on the tree, and you always sit there afterwards.

fail.log: The branch goes anyway, with you on it. You come down in the mud of the yard in a heap of wet leaves at {npc}'s feet, and the two of you look at each other, and {he} starts to laugh through the crying. (-6 health)

choices.text: Stay high, out of sight: it is only a branch

effects.log: It is only a branch. Trees lose branches. But {npc} stands there in the rain until noon looking for you, and you learn something about what a tree is to a child who was born the year it was planted.

events.text: {npc} is of an age to marry, and there is talk in the house of a match with a family in the next valley. You hear it from the tree: the dowry, the bedding, and the chest. A paulownia chest, light and dry, that keeps out the damp and the moths, made from the tree that was planted the year the bride was born. That is what the tree was for. It always was. You are sitting in it.

choices.text: Sit in the tree every day you have left

effects.log: Every dawn, every dusk, on the crooked branch. {npc} knows. {He} brings the dipper out and stands under you without talking now. There is nothing either of you can say that the leaves have not.

choices.text: Choose another tree, now, before it hurts

effects.log: You find a wild paulownia on the ridge above, nobody's, and sit in it for a week. It is a good tree. It is not the tree. You come back to the farmyard on the eighth morning, and {npc} has been looking up every day.

choices.text: Let a leaf fall when {he} asks if it must be cut

mem.note: told me yes

effects.log: You hear {him} ask it, very quietly, alone in the yard at dusk: must it be cut? You let a leaf fall. Yes. That is what trees are for, too. {npc} picks up the leaf and keeps it in {his} sleeve.

events.text: The week before the carpenter is to come, {npc} climbs the paulownia at dawn, which {he} has not done since {he} was small, and sits on the crooked branch beside you, close enough to touch. {He} does not touch you. {He} says: "Tell me what to do." It is the first time {he} has ever waited for an answer.

choices.text: Fly to the ridge and back: there are other trees

mem.note: told me to let the tree go

effects.log: You fly to the wild paulownia on the ridge and back, twice, so {he} can see. There are other trees. {npc} watches, and nods, and climbs down. The tree is cut. The chest is very fine. You sit on the stump the morning of the wedding, and {he} sees you from the bridal palanquin.

choices.text: Stay on the crooked branch, and do not move

mem.note: stayed in my tree

effects.log: You stay. {npc} climbs down and goes into the house and argues with the whole family for two days. A bird of five colours sits in that tree, {he} says; cut it and see. Nobody dares. The chest is made of bought wood, and the tree stands.

choices.text: Drop one of your own feathers into {his} lap

mem.note: gave me a feather from the tree

effects.log: A tail feather, five colours, longer than {his} arm. {npc} holds it and looks at you a long time. The tree is cut, and the chest is made, and inside the lid, where nobody will see it, {he} lays the feather flat and pastes paper over it.

events.text: On the mudflat where the Cinnabar River meets the sea, an old red-crowned crane looks at you for a long time over its own shoulder. Then it walks over on its long black-and-white legs, bends its neck down until its eye is level with yours, and says: "There you are. I have been looking for you for a hundred years. I am your parent."
events.arc: The Crane Who Says It Is Your Parent

choices.text: Believe it

effects.log: You do not look anything like it. It does not matter. Somebody came. You follow it about the mudflat all day, and it shows you which worms not to eat, though you do not eat worms.

choices.text: Ask how, exactly

effects.log: "A dragon and a crane," says the crane, with great dignity, "everybody knows that. That is where your kind comes from. The dragon," it adds, "was not around much." You look for the dragon for years. You never find it. The crane never mentions it again.

choices.text: Say you hatched alone, and nobody came

effects.log: "Exactly," says the crane. "I was late. A hundred years late. Cranes live a thousand years; we are not good with time." It is the worst excuse you have ever heard. You decide to forgive it anyway.

events.text: The crane teaches you, every morning, to stand on one leg. "A bird of quality," it says, "stands on one leg. It shows that it is not in a hurry. It shows it can afford to be still." It stands on one leg for three hours without blinking. You fall into the mud eleven times.
events.arc: The Crane Who Says It Is Your Parent

choices.text: Keep at it until you can

ok.log: On the twelfth morning you stand on one leg for as long as it takes the tide to turn. The crane says nothing. Then it says: "Adequate." From a crane, that is a song.

fail.log: You fall again. The crane sighs, a long sigh from its long neck. "Your dragon side," it says. You decide the dragon side has a lot to answer for. (-2 health)

choices.text: Ask why a bird should not be in a hurry

effects.log: "Because," says the crane, "everything you are hurrying toward is also coming toward you." You think about this for a whole season. It turns out to be true about almost everything except tides.

choices.text: Teach the crane the six steps of your dance in return

effects.log: The crane learns the first four with great solemnity, and the fifth very badly, and refuses the sixth. "A bow," it says, "is for kings." You do not know what a king is yet. You will.

events.text: One autumn the crane does not come back to the mudflat. The other cranes, a long line of them on the far bank, say it went north with the frost and did not come down again. "It was very old," they say. "It thought everyone was its child. It was not right in the head." They say it kindly.
events.arc: The Crane Who Says It Is Your Parent

choices.text: Stand on one leg on its place in the mud, all day

effects.log: You stand on one leg where it used to stand, without falling once, from dawn until the tide comes in over your foot. A bird of quality is not in a hurry. You are not in a hurry to leave.

choices.text: Tell the other cranes it was right

effects.log: "It was my parent," you say. The cranes look at you: drab, five-coloured underneath, nothing like a crane at all. "Yes," says the oldest one at last. "We expect it was." Cranes are not good with time. They are good with kindness.

choices.text: Go north to look for it

effects.log: A long cold flight to the frozen marshes of the north. No crane. Only, on the ice, a single long white feather with a black tip. You keep it for years, in the hollow of whatever tree you sleep in. (-4 health)

events.text: The sparrows of the mill have held a meeting about you. It took all morning and was very loud. They have decided three things, and a spokesparrow comes to your branch to tell you: you are useless, because you will not eat; you are beautiful, which is not your fault; and you are stupid, because of the first thing.

choices.text: Agree with all three

effects.log: The spokesparrow had prepared a long argument and has nowhere to put it. It goes back to the meeting very confused. The meeting goes on until dark.

choices.text: Disagree with the third

effects.log: "I eat," you say, "only not millet." The spokesparrow reports this. The meeting decides that this is the stupidest thing yet, and adds it to the minutes, which are kept in the memory of the oldest sparrow, who forgets them by spring.

choices.text: Ignore the meeting and dance

effects.log: You dance the six steps on the branch while they argue. Half the meeting stops to watch. The other half accuses the first half of being stupid. It is, all things considered, a very sparrow afternoon.

events.text: A hawk over the mill. The sparrows scatter into the thatch, all but a fledgling sparrow caught in the open yard, frozen by the millstone. You are on the roof ridge. You have never fought anything. The hawk is folding its wings to drop.

choices.text: Drop first, between them, all colours open

ok.log: You come down off the roof with your wings and tail spread like a painted fan, and the hawk, which has never seen anything that colour come at it, swerves and goes off over the paddies to think. The fledgling runs into the thatch. Every sparrow saw it.

fail.log: The hawk hits you instead of the fledgling, glances off, and goes away with three of your blue feathers. The fledgling is safe in the thatch. You sit on the millstone, bleeding a little, and every sparrow saw that too. (-8 health)

choices.text: Shriek from the roof, as loud as you can

effects.log: A voice like that has never come out of a mill roof. The hawk looks up, off balance, and the fledgling bolts. You did not know you could make that noise. Neither did the miller, who drops a sack.

choices.text: Stay still. It is not your fight

effects.log: The hawk takes the fledgling and goes. The sparrows come out of the thatch one by one and look at you on the ridge, and do not say anything, which sparrows never do. It is a long autumn.

events.text: One year the sparrows hold another meeting about you, even louder than the first, and come out of it with a new opinion: you are their king. A king of birds. They bow when you land, they make way on the ridge, and they bring you millet, as tribute now, not as medicine. You have done nothing differently at all.

choices.text: Point out that you have done nothing differently

effects.log: "Exactly," says the spokesparrow. "A real king does nothing differently. That is how you can tell." You think about this for decades. It is the most political thing a sparrow has ever said, and it was right.

choices.text: Accept, and refuse the tribute

effects.log: You bow to them and push the millet back, as you did when you were a chick. The sparrows are moved. A king who does not eat the tribute! They tell every sparrow from here to the coast. Sparrows travel.

choices.text: Decline: you are nobody's king

effects.log: They are outraged. They hold another meeting and decide you are useless, beautiful and stupid again. Everyone is much more comfortable. Under the eaves, though, the old ones still make way when you land.

events.text: A goshawk, loose in the hills: young, barred grey, with a little horn tag and a bell and a white goose feather tied in its tail. A falconer's bird, lost from a pheasant hunt. It has been loose a week and it is hungry and furious and it has seen you, a fat colourful thing flying slowly over the open ridge.

choices.text: Dive for the pines and fly low

ok.log: Down off the ridge into the trees, so low your tail brushes the bracken. The hawk follows you in, hits a branch, and gives up with a scream. You learn, in one morning, that the sky is not the safest place for a bird. The trees are.

fail.log: It hits you just as you reach the trees. Talons in your back, a hot pain, a tumble through pine needles, and then it lets go, because a branch hit it too. You lie in the bracken and bleed. Your first wound. You fly low from then on. (-14 health)

choices.text: Climb, higher than it can follow

effects.log: You go up and up, and the hawk comes up under you faster than you knew anything could, and rakes your belly, and falls away because it is a hawk of the low hunt and you are now very high. You are bleeding at a great height, which is lonely. (-8 health)

choices.text: Turn and face it, all colours open

effects.log: The hawk has been trained to come at pheasants, which run. You do not run. You hang in the wind with five colours spread, and the hawk, puzzled, overshoots, circles, and decides you are not a pheasant. Hawks are very literal.

events.text: The goshawk again, thinner. It sits on a dead branch over the pheasant ground, too tired to hunt well, and its jesses have caught round the branch. It cannot fly. Below, a farmer's boy is climbing toward it, and he has a knife: not for the hawk. For the horn tag in its tail with its owner's name on it.

choices.text: Stay and watch what he does

effects.log: He cuts the tag off and throws it in the stream, and takes the hawk home under his jacket as his own. Now nobody can say whose it was. Humans have a name for that, you will learn: cutting off the tag. Pretending you do not know what you know.

choices.text: Shriek, so the falconer's men come

effects.log: You shriek until the beaters in the next valley turn their heads. The boy drops the knife and runs. The falconer's men find their hawk, tag and all, and look up at you a long time. The hawk, too.

choices.text: Free the jesses yourself

effects.log: You work the tangled thong loose with your beak while the hawk watches you with yellow eyes and does not strike. It goes off over the hills with its bell ringing. It does not thank you. It does not hunt you again either. (-4 health)

events.text: A falconer's whole party comes up into your hills in the first snow: men with poles to beat the bushes, a dog, and on the falconer's fist a big young hawk with a hood over its eyes. They are hunting pheasant. They will find you, sooner or later, if you stay in the open: five colours on white snow.

choices.text: Go low, the way the first hawk taught you

effects.log: Low through the pines, in the shadows, never over the white. The party goes home with six pheasants and no idea that a bird worth all the pheasants of the province was ten paces from them all day.

choices.text: Lead them away from the pheasants

ok.log: You cross the open snow once, far up the valley, where they can see you. The hood comes off. The hawk comes. You go into the pines just ahead of it, and lead the whole party round the mountain until dark. The pheasants live. So, barely, do you.

fail.log: The hawk is faster than the first one. You come down in the snow with it on your back, and only the beaters' shouting, as they run to see what in heaven it has caught, makes it let go. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: a falconer's hawk in the first snow

choices.text: Sit very still in a bare paulownia and let them pass

effects.log: They pass right under you. The hooded hawk turns its blind head up toward you as the falconer walks by, and stays turned. It knows. It cannot see you and it knows. Then they are gone.

events.text: In a village under your hill there is a cock: a great red-gold bird with a green-black tail that hangs down behind it like a court robe, and a comb like a king's hat. One misty morning a woodcutter sees you on the ridge, five colours in the fog, and comes down to the village sure that he has seen a phoenix. The village goes looking. They find the cock.
events.arc: The Rooster Who Looks Like You

choices.text: Watch what happens

effects.log: By noon the cock is on a cushion in the headman's yard, and there is a bowl of white rice in front of it, and an old woman is bowing. The cock eats the rice. It is the happiest it has ever been.

choices.text: Fly over the village, low, so they see the real one

ok.log: You go over the rooftops low and slow. Half the village sees you and half does not, and by dusk there is a quarrel in the yard about which bird was the real one. The cock, on its cushion, takes no part. It has rice.

fail.log: The mist is too thick. Nobody looks up. They are all looking at the cock, who is looking at the rice. You fly home feeling, for the first time in your life, slightly ridiculous.

choices.text: Laugh, and leave them to it

effects.log: A village that worships a rooster does no harm to anyone. A phoenix, you think, could do worse than be mistaken for something that crows at dawn and guards the yard. You go back to the bamboo.

events.text: A season later the cock has grown proud. It has a roost of its own now, with paper streamers, and it struts the village lane at noon and pecks the children's ankles and crows outside the headman's window at midnight, because a phoenix may do as it pleases. Nobody dares shoo it. It has begun to look up at your ridge.
events.arc: The Rooster Who Looks Like You

choices.text: Go down and stand in the lane in front of it

effects.log: You land in the lane at noon. The cock stops. It looks at you, five colours and a tail three times its own, and its comb goes slowly pale. Then it walks back to its roost very fast, pretending it meant to. The children laugh. The village quietly takes down the streamers.

choices.text: Leave it be: it is only a cock

effects.log: It is only a cock. You leave it to its glory. In autumn the headman, who has had enough of midnight crowing, eats it at the harvest feast and says it was a very ordinary chicken. Glory is like that.

choices.text: Feel, for a moment, what it would be like to be worshipped

effects.log: You sit on the headman's roof all one afternoon and imagine the rice, the cushion, the bowing. Nobody comes. A roof is not a paulownia, and it leaves a dull taste on your feathers. You do not do it again. (-5 purity)

events.text: Years later the cock is long gone. In its village, at New Year, the women still paste a painting of a red rooster on the gate to keep ghosts away, as everyone does. But in this one village the rooster in the painting has a long tail in five colours, and they say it is because of a bird that came once, or did not. They argue about it.
events.arc: The Rooster Who Looks Like You

choices.text: Sit on the gate post for one New Year dawn

effects.log: A child sees you on the gate post beside the painting and looks from one to the other and back again. "It is the wrong way round," the child says. "The painting is the real one." Children are terrible critics.

choices.text: Leave them their argument

effects.log: An argument about a bird is a good thing for a village to have. It keeps them looking up. You leave them to it.

events.text: Market day in a county town. You are on a roof, which you should not be, because the bamboo grove you were making for is full of cutters and you wanted to see what the noise was. Below, a thin man with a fan is standing in front of a poultry seller's cages, pointing at a big handsome cock. "That bird," he says. "Is that a phoenix?"

choices.text: Stay on the roof and watch

effects.log: "It is a chicken," says the seller. The thin man asks again. And again. Every time he asks it he looks more hopeful. You settle on the warm tiles to watch, and the roof takes a little of the shine off your feathers. (-5 purity)

choices.text: Move to the town's one paulownia and watch from there

ok.log: There is one, in the yard of the county school, half dead, but a paulownia. You watch from its top branch. You cannot hear everything from here, but you can see the thin man's face, which is enough.

fail.log: The school's paulownia is full of crows, who will not make room. You end up on a roof after all. (-5 purity)

choices.text: Leave: a market is no place for you

effects.log: You go back to the hills. Weeks later the whole province is telling the story of the thin man and the cock, and you are sorry, a little, that you missed it.

events.text: "Is it a phoenix?" "It is a chicken." "But is it a phoenix?" Half the market is listening now. On the tenth asking the poultry seller, worn out, waves his hand and says, "Yes, yes, it is a phoenix, if you like." "Then what is the price of a phoenix?" says the thin man. The seller looks at the crowd, and at the fan, and says: "Ten times a chicken." And the thin man pays it.

choices.text: Watch the thin man's face

effects.log: He pays like a man buying a cheap thing, not an expensive one. He is smiling, very slightly, at something that has not happened yet. You understand, watching him, that some humans play a game in which the first move is losing.

choices.text: Watch the cock

effects.log: It sits in the thin man's arms with tremendous dignity, now that it is a phoenix. It has been one for a quarter of an hour. It has never been happier. You feel, oddly, a little proud of it.

choices.text: Watch the crowd

effects.log: Some laugh at the fool who paid ten times. Some look at the cock with a new respect. One old woman looks straight up at the roofs, as if she knows what a real one looks like, and where it might be sitting.

events.text: You follow, from tree to tree, as the thin man carries his phoenix across town to the county office, asks to see the magistrate, and presents it on his knees as a rare gift: a phoenix, for an honest official. The magistrate looks at the cock. The cock looks at the magistrate. "Ten strokes," says the magistrate, "for mocking an officer of the state with a chicken."

choices.text: Wince at every stroke

effects.log: Ten strokes of the paddle in the yard, and the thin man yells at every one, very loudly, and very convincingly, and at the tenth he stops yelling and begins to weep, which is better still. You are not sure it hurt as much as all that.

choices.text: Watch the magistrate instead

effects.log: The magistrate is bored and a little ashamed and wants his lunch. Nobody who has seen a real phoenix gives that order. Nobody who has seen one would need to. You make a note of the kind of face it is.

choices.text: Go down into the yard so the magistrate sees a real one

effects.log: You land on the yard wall. The magistrate sees you. His mouth opens. The thin man, face down on the bench, sees the magistrate's face and nearly laughs out loud. Then you are gone, and the clerks are sent out with nets for a week, and catch nothing.

events.text: Then the thin man, tears on his face, tells the magistrate how it was: the seller said it was a phoenix, ten times over, in front of the whole market, and took a phoenix's price. The seller is sent for. The whole market comes as witness. The seller is made to pay back the price of a phoenix, and the price of ten strokes on top. The thin man walks out of the office with ten times his money and his cock, and laughs all the way down the street.

choices.text: Laugh with him, from the tree

effects.log: You laugh in your own voice, a strange high laugh from the paulownia, and the thin man stops in the road and looks up. He sees you. He bows, very deeply, with the cock under his arm, one swindler to another. You are not a swindler. You bow back anyway.

choices.text: Feel sorry for the poultry seller

effects.log: He only said yes to make a madman go away. Now he has lost a month's trade for it. You learn from his face that the word phoenix costs money in this country. One day it will cost more than that.

choices.text: Think about the cock

effects.log: It was a phoenix for an hour, a chicken for ten strokes, and then a rich man's chicken for the rest of its life. Nobody asked it once. You think that might be the whole story of what it means, among humans, to be called a phoenix.

events.text: A schoolhouse at the end of a poor village: one room, a paper window, a lamp that burns late. The teacher, a thin scholar who failed the state examination twice and has stopped trying, is planting a paulownia sapling by the door with a borrowed hoe. "I plant you," {npc} tells the sapling, very seriously, "to see the phoenix."

choices.text: Watch from the ridge, and say nothing

effects.log: You are too young, and much too shy, to go down to a human who says your name to a stick. You watch {npc} water it with a dipper, and bow to it, and go in. The lamp burns until the third watch.

choices.text: Land on the schoolhouse roof, just once, at dusk

effects.log: You land on the thatch for a moment and fly off again before you can think. {npc} comes out with the lamp and looks at the roof and the sapling and the sky, and goes back in, and does not sleep at all that night. (-5 purity)

choices.text: Note the tree, for when it is grown

effects.log: A paulownia grows fast. In five years it will hold a bird. You make a note of the place, the way the crane taught you: everything you are hurrying toward is also coming toward you.

events.text: The scholar's paulownia is as tall as the schoolhouse now. Every evening, when the children have gone home, {npc} sits under it with a book that {he} does not read, and looks up into the leaves. You know, because you have been sitting in the next valley's pines and looking back.

choices.text: Go, at last, and sit in it

mem.note: came to my paulownia

ok.log: You land in the top of {his} tree one evening and {npc} looks up and sees you and does not move, does not call, does not do anything at all, for as long as it takes the light to go. Then {he} bows, very low, and goes in, and you hear {him} weeping, and it is not sad.

fail.log: You get as far as the schoolhouse wall and lose your nerve, and turn back to the pines. {npc}, under the tree, saw a flash of colour going away, and tells {him}self it was a jay.

choices.text: Stay away: you are not ready to be seen

effects.log: You are not. To be seen by someone who has waited a whole life is a heavy thing for a young bird to carry. You stay in the pines. {npc} reads {his} book that {he} does not read.

choices.text: Sit in the pines and sing, so {he} can hear but not see

effects.log: Three notes, across the valley, at dusk. {npc} stands up so fast the book falls in the dirt. {He} stands there until dark, listening for more. There is no more. You were too shy for more.

events.text: Late at night, from the ridge, you can see the scholar's lamp. Every night of every season. The children come and go, the village gets no richer, {npc} gets greyer, and the lamp burns. Once, passing low in the dark, you hear {him} reciting, to nobody, the old line: the phoenix does not come; I am finished.

choices.text: Fly past the window, once, in the lamplight

mem.note: went past my window

effects.log: A shadow with a long tail across the paper, there and gone. The recitation stops. A long silence. Then the voice goes on, but it has changed the line: the phoenix does not come, it says, and then, very quietly, yet.

choices.text: Leave a long feather in the tree

mem.note: left a five-coloured feather in my tree

effects.log: In the morning there is a tail feather caught in the scholar's paulownia, five colours, long as an arm. {npc} takes it down very carefully and pins it to the wall of the schoolroom, and every child for years is told it is real, and does not believe it.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge and watch the lamp

effects.log: You watch the lamp until it goes out at the fourth watch. You are learning something you will not have words for until much later: that some people are kept alive by waiting for you, and that coming would end the waiting.

events.text: A clear night, a full moon, and you have flown over the schoolhouse late. The scholar's paulownia stands bare in the autumn cold, and the moon has caught on its top branch, exactly where a bird would sit. {npc} is under the tree with a brush and a scrap of paper, looking at the moon on the empty branch, and writing.

choices.text: Land on the branch, in front of the moon

mem.note: came to the branch under the moon

effects.log: You come down onto the branch, black against the moon. {npc} stops writing. The brush shakes. {He} does not tear up the poem. {He} only adds one word at the end of the last line, and you never learn which word it was.

choices.text: Stay away, and let {him} write it

effects.log: Three lines about a paulownia planted to see the phoenix, and a phoenix that does not come, and only the moon on the empty branch. In a hundred years every child in the country will know them. Nobody will know they were written about you, staying away.

choices.text: Sing, very softly, from the dark

mem.note: heard the phoenix sing under the moon

ok.log: One phrase, from the dark of the ridge. {npc} lifts {his} head. Then {he} writes the three lines anyway, about a phoenix that does not come, because a poet writes the poem {he} has, not the one {he} was given.

fail.log: The wind takes your voice the wrong way, down the valley. {npc} hears nothing, and writes three lines about an empty branch, and they are the saddest lines anyone has written in that province.

events.text: The scholar's three lines are sung in the market now, to a tune somebody made up for them. A boy herding a cow sings them under your tree: the paulownia planted to see the phoenix, the phoenix that does not come, the bright moon on the empty branch. He sings them very badly, and very sadly, and has no idea what they mean.

choices.text: Answer the song from the tree

effects.log: The boy stops. The cow stops. You sing the last phrase back to him, properly. He runs home leaving the cow, and the cow, with nothing better to do, stands under the tree and listens to the rest.

choices.text: Let it go: the lines are not about you any more

effects.log: Every child who learns them thinks of their own empty branch. That is what lines are for. You are only the first bird they were about, and that is a small thing to be, and a large one.

events.text: You notice it when you turn round on a log: a wren behind you. Behind the wren, two buntings. Behind them, a lost young magpie that has fallen out of a nest and is too proud to say so. They are walking along the log after you in a line, and when you stop, they stop.

choices.text: Walk on, and see how far they follow

effects.log: To the end of the log, along the stream, up the bank, into the bamboo. They follow the whole way. You turn round in the bamboo and there are seven now. None of them knows why. Neither do you.

choices.text: Tell them to go home

effects.log: They look at each other. The wren goes home. The buntings go home. The magpie, who has no home, stays. It follows you for a whole season, stealing things, and then one morning it is grown and gone.

choices.text: Dance the six steps for them, since they are here

effects.log: You dance on the log, and they watch in their line, and at the bow they all bow too, badly, falling over each other. It is the first time anyone has watched you dance. You find you do not mind.

events.text: An old crow sits on the dead branch above your log and watches the line of small birds behind you for a long time. It is the oldest crow you have ever seen, grey at the beak. It fed its own old parent, it tells you, when the parent was too old to hunt, as crows do. It knows things. "I have seen this before," it says. "A long time ago. A bird the little ones followed. It went to the king's city, in the end."

choices.text: Ask what happened to it

effects.log: "It sat on a palace roof," says the crow, "and the king came out and wept, and there was peace for years. And then the king grew old, and the bird stayed too long." The crow will not say any more. It knows about staying too long. It fed its parent.

choices.text: Ask if the bird was like you

effects.log: "No," says the crow. "It was not a chick. It was very large, with a long tail, and it did not walk on logs." It looks at you. "But it walked on logs once, I suppose. Everything does."

choices.text: Say you will never go to any king's city

effects.log: The crow laughs, a crow's laugh, like a dry branch snapping. "Everyone the little ones follow goes to the king's city," it says. "The only question is when you leave."

events.text: You are grown now, and the little birds still come. Not in a line on a log: in a cloud. Where you land in the bamboo, the wrens and buntings and tits of the whole grove settle round you within the hour, and stop quarrelling, and preen. Where you leave, they scatter. You did not ask for this either.

choices.text: Leave them be: it is not your doing

effects.log: Woodcutters notice. A grove where every bird is sitting still and quiet is a grove where something is. They do not see you. They see the birds, and go home, and say the grove is lucky.

choices.text: Lead them, once, on a long flight

effects.log: You go up out of the bamboo and the whole grove comes up after you, a hundred small birds, and you lead them in a long loop over three villages. Every farmer in the valley stops work to look. It is the first time anyone has seen it. It will not be the last.

choices.text: Go somewhere they cannot follow, for quiet

effects.log: High on a bare ridge where no wren goes, you sit alone for a week. It is good. It is also, you find, a little too quiet now. You have been spoiled. You go back down.

events.text: The bamboo stem you land on is wet. Not with rain: with something brown and thick that takes your feet and does not give them back. Birdlime. Somebody has smeared every good perch in this grove with it. You pull, and your feet stay where they are, and a tail feather touches the stem and stays too. Down the path, a man with a cage on his back is whistling.

choices.text: Pull with everything you have

ok.log: You come away from the stem leaving half the down off your feet and two tail feathers behind for the bird-catcher to sell. You sit in a stream for an hour washing the stuff off. You will look at every wet perch for the rest of your life. (-8 health)

fail.log: The more you pull, the more of you the lime holds. When the whistling man comes round the bend you are stuck by both feet and one wing, upside down. He stops. His mouth opens. He has never in his life caught anything like you. (-5 health)

choices.text: Keep very still and wait for him

effects.log: Struggling only wastes feathers. You hang there with as much dignity as a bird stuck to a stick can have, which is some. The bird-catcher comes round the bend and stops dead. He has never in his life caught anything like you.

choices.text: Sing, loud, to warn the grove

effects.log: Every bird in the grove goes up at once, a hundred wings, and leaves the limed stems empty. The bird-catcher, coming round the bend, finds the whole grove clean of birds but one. He stares at you. It is a fair trade, he thinks, for a whole day's lime.

events.text: The bird-catcher has you in a cage on a back-frame, wrapped in a cloth, on the road to market. Through a gap in the cloth you see a village, a well, and a child at the well with a water jar: {npc}, small and thin in a patched jacket, who has seen your tail hanging out of the cloth and has put down the jar.

choices.text: Look at the child, and hope

effects.log: {npc} runs after the bird-catcher, catches the catcher by the sleeve, and asks what is in the cage. A pheasant, says the catcher. {npc} says it is not a pheasant. The catcher laughs. {npc} holds up two coppers, everything {he} has, and says: then sell me the pheasant.

choices.text: Stay still: a child cannot help you

effects.log: You stay still. But {npc} runs after the bird-catcher anyway, and catches the catcher by the sleeve, and holds up two coppers, everything {he} has, and says: let it go. It is not yours. It is not anybody's.

choices.text: Shake the cage so the child sees your colours

effects.log: You shake the cloth off one wing. Five colours, in a market road. {npc} goes white and then runs, not away but after the bird-catcher, and catches the catcher by the sleeve, and holds up two coppers.

events.text: The bird-catcher looks at {npc}'s two coppers, and at the cage, and at {npc} again. Two coppers is nothing. What is in the cage is worth a magistrate's favour, or a feather-crown-maker's whole season. But {npc} is looking at the catcher the way you look at someone about to do the right thing, and the catcher is not used to that.

choices.text: Look at the bird-catcher too, the same way

mem.note: paid two coppers to free the bird

ok.log: Two of you, looking at the catcher the same way. The catcher takes the coppers, swearing, and opens the cage, and you go up out of it into the sky over the village. {npc} watches you all the way to the hills. The bird-catcher watches {npc}, and much later takes up honest work.

mem.note: paid two coppers and a beating to free the bird

fail.log: The catcher laughs and walks on. {npc} runs after the cage, and grabs the cage, and in the struggle the little door springs open and you are out and up, leaving feathers, and {npc} gets a cuff on the ear and two coppers kept. {He} does not mind. {He} saw you go. (-6 health)

choices.text: Break the cage door with your beak during the argument

mem.note: held the bird-catcher talking while the bird got free

ok.log: The bamboo bars give while the catcher is still laughing at the coppers. You are out and over the well before anyone turns. {npc} still has {his} two coppers, and the best story in the village.

mem.note: paid two coppers to free the bird

fail.log: You only bloody your beak on the bars. In the end it is the two coppers that do it: the catcher takes them, because a crowd is gathering, and a catcher who refuses a child in front of a crowd does not sell much in that village again. You go up, bleeding a little. (-8 health)

events.text: Years later you fly over the village with the well. {npc} is grown, drawing water with a child of {his} own beside {him}. As your shadow goes over the well {npc} looks up, and puts down the jar, and points, and says something to the child that makes the child laugh and look up too.

choices.text: Circle the well once, low

mem.note: came back over the well

effects.log: Once round, low enough to see the face. {npc} stands with both hands up as if to catch something. That child will grow up hearing about two coppers, and believing it, which is rarer.

choices.text: Drop a seed into the well-water, as thanks

mem.note: dropped something into my well

effects.log: One bamboo seed, into the bucket as it comes up. {npc} finds it and does not know what it is, and keeps it anyway, in the same box as two old coppers that {he} never spent.

events.text: Lime on the bamboo again, a different grove, a different catcher. You know the look of it now: a stem too shiny for the weather, a smell like boiled bark. A family of buntings is about to land on it.

choices.text: Land first on a safe stem, and shriek

effects.log: The buntings veer off into the bracken. The catcher, coming round with his cage, finds an empty grove and a bird of five colours on an unlimed stem looking at him. He goes home and tells his wife he is giving it up. He does not. But he limes fewer stems.

choices.text: Wipe the stems with leaves, one by one

effects.log: A morning's work, beak and leaves, and every stem in the grove dull again. You have lime on your face for a week. Nothing gets caught in that grove that season, and the catcher, very puzzled, moves on. (-3 health)

choices.text: Leave the grove to the catcher

effects.log: It is his living. You fly on. The buntings land, and you do not look back to see what happens. You are not sure, later, that it was the right thing. You are sure it was the easy one.

events.text: A drought year. No rain since the plum blossom, and the paddies are cracked like old pots. Every sweet spring you know is a damp stain on the rock. In the valley, the villagers carry an old pig's head up to the hill and pray for rain. You are so thirsty your tongue sticks to your beak.

choices.text: Go thirsty, and fly the country for a spring

ok.log: Nine days of flying, and on the ninth, in a cave on a hill nobody climbs, one thread of sweet water coming out of the rock. You drink it drop by drop for an hour. It is the best water you will ever drink. (-6 health, +2 purity)

fail.log: Nine days of flying, and nothing. You come home with your feathers dull and your tongue like leather, and sit on the branch and wait for rain. (-14 health)

choices.text: Drink from the ditch by the road

effects.log: Brown water, warm, with a taste of ox and road. It goes down, and it keeps you alive, and something in your breast feathers turns its face away. (-5 purity)

choices.text: Drink the dew off the paulownia leaves at dawn

effects.log: One drop a leaf, a hundred leaves. It is slow and it is not enough. But it is clean. A phoenix that drinks dew, you think, is very nearly keeping its word. (-4 health)

events.text: The drought goes on. In the village the people dig a new well, deeper, all of them together, and the headman's old mother sits by it all night with a lamp. At dawn they hit water: cloudy, then clear. They hang a bucket and a gourd on the well-frame for anyone who passes. You are passing.

choices.text: Drink from the well. It was dug for anyone

effects.log: It is not a sweet spring. It is a village's well, dug with all their hands, and given. It goes down well. The thing in your breast feathers frowns, but only a little. (-3 purity)

choices.text: Refuse it, and bow to the old woman with the lamp

effects.log: You bow, from the well-frame. The old woman bows back without thinking, as to a guest, and only then sees what you are. She tells nobody. She sits by the well every night after that, with the lamp, in case you come again. (-5 health)

events.text: The rain comes at last, all at once, in a black wall over the hills. The paddies drink. The ditches overflow. And three days after the rain, the sweet spring under the old rock begins again, a little, then more, and the taste is the same as it ever was, as if nothing had happened.

choices.text: Drink, and remember the ditch

effects.log: It tastes the way it always did. You do not. You drink slowly, and remember the dry weeks, and what you did in them, and the spring does not judge you. Springs do not. That is your job.

choices.text: Dance in the rain on the bare rock

effects.log: Six steps and the bow, soaked through, on the rock over the spring, while the whole valley drinks. A farmer under a straw rain cape sees a bird dancing in a downpour and decides, sensibly, that he has been in the sun too long.

events.text: You come back to the wild paulownia on the ridge where you have slept winter after winter, and it is a stump. The smell of the cut is still fresh. Down the slope an old man and a boy are dragging the trunk on a sledge, and the old man, {npc}, keeps stopping to knock on it with {his} knuckles and listen, like a doctor at a chest.

choices.text: Follow the trunk down the hill

effects.log: To a workshop yard where the roofs are covered with pale planks drying in the sun, years of them, and the air smells of sawdust and lacquer. {npc} is a zither-maker. Your tree is going to be the sound-board of a zither. It will be years before it is dry enough to sing.

choices.text: Sit on the stump and grieve for it
