effects.log: You sit on the stump through a cold night. All those winters in that tree. In the morning you find you remember the exact shape of its branches, and that it was only a tree, and that you will never forgive {npc} at all, and then, by noon, that you already have.

choices.text: Scream at the old man from the sky

effects.log: You come down over the sledge shrieking. The boy drops the rope and runs. {npc} only looks up, and nods, as if apologising to a customer. "A good tree," {he} says. "I knew someone was sitting in it. It rings."

events.text: Years later, at a village feast, someone plays a new twelve-string zither under a lantern: pale paulownia wood, silk strings, the bridges like a line of wild geese. You hear the first note from three valleys away. It is your tree. Every winter you slept in it is in the sound, and something else too: your own voice, the one you used on that ridge at dawn, coming back out of the wood.

choices.text: Come and sit in the dark by the feast and listen

effects.log: You listen until the lantern burns down. The player does not know why everyone is so quiet tonight. You know. The tree was listening to you for all those winters, and it remembered. Wood is like that, if it is good wood.

choices.text: Sing along with it, from the trees

ok.log: The zither and you, one voice in the wood and one in the dark. The player stops. You stop. The player starts again, slowly, and you come in, and for one song the whole feast forgets to eat. Nobody ever plays that zither again without someone saying: you should have heard it that night.

fail.log: You sing a note too high, and the player loses the tune, and the whole feast turns to look at the dark trees. You stop. The zither starts again. You let it sing alone. It was its song tonight, not yours.

choices.text: Find {npc}, and look at {him}

mem.note: came to hear the zither

effects.log: {npc} is at the back of the feast, very old now, eyes closed. {He} feels you looking and opens them and finds you in the dark at once. {He} nods, the way {he} did at the sledge. You nod back. A tree is a good price for that sound. You did not choose to pay it, but it is paid.

events.text: Spring. A sapling has come up by the zither-maker's stump on the ridge, from the old roots: a paulownia shoot with three leaves as wide as your wing. Paulownias do that. You cut them and they come back.

choices.text: Sit by it and keep the goats off

effects.log: A whole spring of chasing goats. By autumn the shoot is taller than you. In a few years it will hold you. You will sleep in it, and one day somebody will cut it and make it sing. That is the bargain, and you take it.

choices.text: Look for a tree nobody will cut

effects.log: You find one in a gorge so steep no sledge could ever come. It is crooked and will never sing. You sleep in it, safe, and dream of zithers.

events.text: Your first moult. A blue feather comes loose from your wing over a forest path and spins down and down, end over end, and lands at the feet of {npc}, a small child gathering acorns. {npc} picks it up and holds it to the light, and turns it, and the blue goes green and back to blue.

choices.text: Watch from the branch

mem.note: found a blue feather on the path

effects.log: {npc} looks up into the branches for a long time and does not see you. {He} puts the acorns down on the path, all of them, and carries the feather home in both hands, as if it were water.

choices.text: Let {him} see you

mem.note: saw the bird whose feather it was

effects.log: {npc} looks up and finds you. You look down. {He} holds up the feather, as if asking whether {he} should give it back. You shake out your wing, the way birds do. Keep it. {He} understands at once. Children understand that sort of thing.

choices.text: Drop a second one

mem.note: let a second feather fall for me

effects.log: A second, a red one this time, falling on purpose. {npc} catches it in mid-air and stares at the two of them, blue and red, and then at the sky. That night the feathers go into a little wooden box that held {his} grandmother's hairpins.

events.text: You see the box years later, through a paper window with a hole in it: a small lacquered box on a shelf, and {npc}, grown taller, opening it at night to look at what is inside. The blue has not faded at all. {npc} closes the box, carefully, the way you close a door on a sleeping child.

choices.text: Leave another feather on the windowsill

mem.note: another feather on my windowsill

effects.log: A small black one, from your neck. In the morning {npc} finds it and goes quite still, and then looks out at every tree in the village, one by one. The box has three now. It will be kept a long time.

choices.text: Sing once outside the window

mem.note: heard the bird outside my window

effects.log: {npc} opens the window and you are gone. But {he} heard. {He} holds the box on {his} knees until morning. You will see that box again at a wedding many years from now, opened in front of everyone, and you will know it at once.

choices.text: Let the box keep its own secret

effects.log: You fly on. A feather is a small thing to lose. To someone else, it seems, it can be the whole of a childhood. You do not quite understand that yet. You will, at the wedding.

events.text: In the village with the box, the other children have heard. One of them, a bigger child, takes the box off the shelf when nobody is home and runs to the river with it, to see whether the feathers float. {npc} comes home and finds the shelf empty, and goes white, and runs.

choices.text: Find the bigger child at the river first

mem.note: brought the box back from the river

ok.log: You land on the bank beside the thief, who has the box open and one feather between finger and thumb, and simply look. The child puts the feather back, shuts the box, and runs. {npc} finds the box on the bank, closed, safe, and a bird of five colours leaving.

mem.note: only the blue feather came back from the river

fail.log: You are too late. Two feathers are already on the current. But the blue one, the first one, you snatch out of the water as it goes under the bridge, and you leave it on {npc}'s doorstep, wet. It dries. It is still blue. (-3 health)

choices.text: Leave it: they are only feathers, and you have many

effects.log: They are only feathers. {npc} finds the box on the riverbank, empty, and does not cry, and keeps the box. Some people keep the box. Some people are like that. You learn later that {he} never forgave the bigger child, and never needed to fill the box again.

events.text: A traveller sleeps under your paulownia: {npc}, a young swordsman of the second rank with a cloth-wrapped sword and a road in {his} sandals. Before {he} sleeps {he} eats cold rice from a bundle, and looks up into your tree, and says to the dark, "Hungry? There is plenty," and sets a little of the rice on a root.

choices.text: Do not touch the rice, but stay

mem.note: shared rice with the tree

effects.log: You stay on your branch all night, watching {npc} sleep with one hand on the sword. In the morning the rice is still on the root. {npc} looks at it and laughs. "Proud," {he} says to the tree. "Me too." And goes on.

choices.text: Come down and push the rice back to {him}

mem.note: gave my rice back, a bird of five colours

effects.log: You come down off the branch and nudge the rice back across the root to {his} hand. {npc} sits up and stares at you for a long time, the sword forgotten. "Not rice," {he} says at last. "No. I suppose you would not." {He} eats it alone, very slowly.

choices.text: Keep watch for {him} through the night

mem.note: kept watch over me

effects.log: Wolves come to the edge of the road at the second watch. You shriek once, from the branch, and they go. {npc} sleeps through it. In the morning {he} finds wolf tracks in a circle round the tree, at a distance, and does not understand them at all.

events.text: The swordsman comes back along the road the next year, and the year after, always to your tree, always at dusk, always with a little rice that {he} sets on the root and you never eat. {npc} talks to the tree now: about the fights, the sects, a friend killed on the road. {He} is getting better with the sword. {He} is getting sadder.

choices.text: Listen, as you would to the daughter of the house

mem.note: listened to me every year

effects.log: A human who talks to a tree is saying things they cannot say to a human. You listen, and the rice goes cold on the root, and {npc} sleeps better under you than anywhere else on the road. {He} tells you so.

choices.text: Sing {him} to sleep

mem.note: sang me to sleep

effects.log: Three notes, low, from the leaves. {npc} goes still, and then {he} lies back with the sword across {his} chest and is asleep before the fourth. In the morning {he} does not mention it. {He} only leaves twice as much rice.

choices.text: Drop a leaf on the sword when {he} talks about killing

mem.note: dropped a leaf on my sword

effects.log: A wide leaf, landing on the cloth-wrapped blade just as {npc} says the name of the man {he} means to kill. {He} looks at the leaf a long time. {He} does not kill the man, that year. {He} says it was the leaf.

events.text: One autumn {npc} does not come. The next autumn, a stranger walks the road and stops at your tree and sets down a little bowl of rice on the root and a sword wrapped in cloth beside it, and bows, and goes on without a word. You know the sword.

choices.text: Keep the sword under your tree

effects.log: It lies at the foot of the paulownia under the leaves for years, and the rust takes it, and nobody on that road ever touches it. Travellers sleep a little further from the tree than they need to, out of respect for something they do not know about.

choices.text: Sing the three notes over it, once

effects.log: Three notes, low, the ones that put {npc} to sleep. The stranger, a little way down the road, stops and turns round and stands there. Then goes on. Somebody told the stranger about this tree. Now the stranger knows it was true.

events.text: The store is empty. The crack in the rock where you keep your bamboo seed has nothing in it but dust and a beetle, and it is the first month of the year, and every grove you know is bare. Below, the farmyards have millet in every bin. A phoenix, the old saying will go, may fly a thousand li hungry, and not peck millet.
events.arc: Lean Years of the Young Bird

choices.text: Fast. Fly the thousand li

effects.log: You fast. You fly the groves with nothing in your crop, and sleep with your head under your wing, and in spring, very thin, you are still what you were. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck millet, just this year

effects.log: A farmyard at dawn, a spill of millet by the mill door, and you eat. It keeps you alive. It also keeps, for a long time after, a dull place in your feathers that no spring washes out quickly. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Search the old flowering slopes for missed seed

ok.log: Under the dead stems of a grove that flowered long ago, in a crack the rats never found, a little heap of old seed. Hard, stale, right. You live on it until spring. (-4 health)

fail.log: Every crack picked clean by rats years ago. You fly home empty and sit out the winter on nothing. (-12 health)

variants: Empty. The hollow where you keep your bamboo seed holds nothing but frost, it is the first month of the year, and every grove you know is bare. Below, the mill has spilled millet in the snow. A phoenix, the old saying will go, may fly a thousand li hungry, and not peck millet.

The seed store is dust. The groves are bare, the wind is cutting, and you are very young. Down in the farmyard the hens are fat on millet. A phoenix, the old saying will go, may fly a thousand li hungry, and not peck millet.

events.text: A lean year again. The cold has got into your hollow bones and stayed. The sparrows of the mill, who remember you, line up on your branch with their beakfuls of millet, the way they did when you were small, and look at you with tremendous concern.

choices.text: Refuse, and thank them, as you did then

effects.log: One bow for each sparrow. They take their millet away again, discussing your madness. You fast. In spring there are fewer sparrows on the branch, but the ones who come still bow. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take theirs: they offered it

effects.log: Eaten from a sparrow's beak, it is still millet. The sparrows are overjoyed. You are alive. Under your breast feathers something has gone quiet, the way a house goes quiet when a guest is offended. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Sleep through the worst of it in your hollow

effects.log: You fold into the hollow of the paulownia with your tail round you and let the winter go over. You wake thin and dizzy and clean. (-6 health)

events.text: Empty again. You are thinner than a bird your age should be, and you know what the sparrows would say: you eat what we eat now. The farmyards are full. The groves are bare. It is the first month, and the year is long.
events.arc: Lean Years of the Young Bird

choices.text: Fast, and go to the sweet spring, and drink only that

effects.log: Water and nothing else, for a season. It is not food. But it is clean, and you are cleaner for it, and in spring a grove in the south gives up a little old seed to the first bird there. You are the first bird there. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck millet, and do not look at the sparrows

effects.log: You eat with your eyes shut. The sparrows watch. They do not say anything. That is how you know how far you have come down. (-8 purity)

events.text: The wind brings it before any bird does: a smell like dry straw and rice flour, from the south. Then the birds bring it, wren to tit to magpie: the bamboo of the southern province is in flower. All of it. All at once. It has not happened in that province in the lifetime of anything that can remember.

choices.text: Fly south at once

effects.log: Three days of flying, and then a whole province of pale bamboo, nodding, and the seed coming down on the wind like grain off a threshing floor. You gather until your crop aches. It is your first Bamboo Year, and you do not quite believe it is real.

choices.text: Fly south, and go to the old cutters' village first

effects.log: You stop at the village of the old clump to see. Their bamboo is flowering too. The cutters stand under it with their sickles hanging. You gather there, where you began, and the old cutter, very old now, looks up and says, "Ah. You again."

choices.text: Stay. There will be other flowerings

effects.log: There will. You are young, and you are not sure yet that you need so much. Other birds go south. You stay with your little store and the sweet spring. Later you will wish you had gone.

events.text: In the flowering province the rats have come. They are everywhere under the bamboo, fat on the seed, bold, more of them every week. The villagers there do not know yet what is coming for their granaries. You do. Rats follow the seed.

choices.text: Gather fast and go, before the rats are worse

effects.log: You fill the store and leave. Behind you the rats spread out of the dying groves into the paddies. It is not your doing. It is also, a little, your harvest that fed them.

choices.text: Warn the villagers the only way you can

ok.log: You sit on the granary roof of the biggest village every dawn for a week, shrieking, until an old woman says that the bird is telling them something about the granary. They move the rice up into the rafters and stop the holes with clay. That winter, they are the only village in the province that eats.

fail.log: They shoo you off the granary with poles and call you an evil omen, because the bamboo is dying and here is a strange bird. That winter they starve, and remember the strange bird, and are not grateful.

choices.text: Hunt the rats in the grove

effects.log: You come down on them in the stems again and again. There are too many. You thin them, a little, and come away with a bitten foot and the knowledge that no bird stops a Bamboo Year. (-5 health)

events.text: On a winter evening the grandmother of the house sits under your paulownia with {npc} at the old woman's feet and tells the old story of the family: how, generations ago, a paulownia planted for a daughter of this house was to be cut for the bride's wedding chest, and two birds of five colours sang in it at sunrise, and one of the household stood up at the wedding talks, red to the ears, and begged for it to be spared. "That is why we plant them," the grandmother says. "For the birds. And that is why we never cut them in the week the birds are singing."

choices.text: Sing, very softly, from the high branch

mem.note: sang during the old story

effects.log: Three notes. The grandmother stops in the middle of a word. {npc} looks up, and then at the grandmother, who has told this story every winter of {his} life and never quite believed it, and who now puts a hand over the mouth that told it.

choices.text: Stay still and hear the whole story

effects.log: You hear it to the end: a human, long ago, who looked up at two birds and asked for one more year for a tree. You did not know you owed anyone this branch. You do. Somewhere in the past of this house there is a face you have never seen, and you sit in its kindness every morning.

choices.text: Drop a leaf into the grandmother's lap

effects.log: One wide leaf, spinning down. The grandmother picks it up and turns it over as if there might be writing on it. There is not. It is kept anyway, pressed in the family register, between the names.

events.text: After you are free, the bird-catcher sits down on the edge of the well and laughs until he coughs. "The second time," he tells the village, which has gathered. "The second time in my life a child has stood in front of me with two coppers for one of these. The first was when I was a boy apprenticed to my uncle, and the brat stood there with two coins and that same face. My uncle let it go. I swore I never would." He looks at the empty cage. "Two coppers. It must be the price."

choices.text: Come back and sit on the well-frame, once

effects.log: You land on the well-frame beside him. The catcher stops laughing. He looks at you a long time, a bird he has caught and lost and will never catch again, and then he takes off his hat, which nobody in that village has ever seen him do for anyone.

choices.text: Fly on, and think about the first child

effects.log: Another life, another bird, the same two coppers. You think of a child you never met who taught a bird-catcher's apprentice that some things have a price of two coppers and no more. It has taken a whole lifetime to reach you. It reached you in time.

events.text: In the next grove a family of bird-catchers has a rule nobody outside the family understands: every catcher carries a small jar of lamp oil on the belt, beside the lime. If what the lime takes is a bird of five colours, they say, you oil its feet and let it go, and you do not tell anyone. It was a child who taught the grandfather that, they say, with a lamp-oil jar and both hands, a long time ago. Today a young catcher of that family finds you on a stem.

choices.text: Hold still for the oil

effects.log: Careful fingers, cold oil, and your feet come off the stem one toe at a time. The young catcher does not look at your colours once, out of manners. When you are free the catcher bows to you and goes back to liming stems for buntings, which is a living. (-2 health)

choices.text: Sing the family a thank-you before you go

effects.log: You sing from the top of the grove after the oil, three notes. The young catcher goes home and tells the grandmother, who nods as if she had been expecting it for sixty years.

events.text: {npc}'s family has a second box. You see it the night {npc} sets them side by side on the floor: the new one, with your feathers in it, and an old one, black with age, that came down from a grandparent's grandparent. In the old one, on faded silk, lies one long blue feather, stuck at the quill with a crust of old birdlime. Not yours. It is the same blue.

choices.text: Look at the old feather a long time

mem.note: looked at the old feather

effects.log: A bird of your kind, caught on a lime-stick once, long ago, and a child of this family who stood in front of the sticks with both arms out. You are not the first of your kind these people have kept a feather for. You fly home very quietly.

choices.text: Leave a feather of yours beside the old one

mem.note: left a new feather beside the old one

effects.log: In the morning {npc} finds a new blue feather lying across the lid of the old box, as if laid there to keep the old one company. {npc} does not move it. Two blues, one old, one new, and nobody in the house can say which is the brighter.
